T1A01.explanation: Part 97 exists to advance radio technical and communication skills, emergency readiness, and international goodwill—unlike CB or FRS, which serve mass personal radio use.

T1A02.explanation: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) writes and enforces Part 97 rules; the ARRL is a private membership organization, not a government regulator.

T1A03.explanation: Standard phonetics (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie) prevent similar-sounding letters from getting confused over noisy voice channels, so the FCC encourages—but never requires—them on phone.

T1A04.explanation: The FCC no longer mails paper licenses; official notice arrives via an FCC email containing a link to download your official license grant PDF.

T1A05.explanation: Your exam-day CSCE only proves you passed the test—an operator/primary license isn't officially granted until it appears in the FCC ULS database.

T1A06.explanation: Worldwide automatic 10-meter propagation beacons transmit exclusively inside the 100 kHz window from 28.200 to 28.300 MHz, right below Technician SSB voice.

T1A07.explanation: Part 97 draws the legal boundary of space at 50 km: any amateur station operating more than 50 km above Earth's surface is a space station, crewed or uncrewed.

T1A08.explanation: Rather than assigning repeater frequencies from Washington, the FCC relies on locally recognized Volunteer Frequency Coordinators to recommend channel pairs that avoid interference.

T1A09.explanation: Frequency coordinators are not appointed by the FCC—they are selected directly by local or regional amateurs whose stations are eligible to be repeaters or auxiliary links.

T1A10.explanation: Because RACES supports official government civil-defense operations, acting as a RACES control operator requires both an FCC ham license and enrollment certified by a civil defense organization.

T1A11.explanation: Deliberately transmitting on top of or jamming other stations—willful or malicious interference—is strictly illegal across every amateur band.

T1B01.explanation: Technicians get HF single-sideband (SSB) voice privileges in one dedicated window: 28.300 to 28.500 MHz on the 10-meter band.

T1B02.explanation: The ISS ham station uses standard 2-meter VHF frequencies, so any Technician or higher licensee can talk to astronauts without special NASA permission.

T1B03.explanation: The 6-meter band spans 50 to 54 MHz (300 / 6 = 50), making 52.525 MHz—the 6m national FM simplex calling channel—the only frequency inside the band.

T1B04.explanation: The 2-meter band runs from 144 to 148 MHz (300 / 2 is ~150), with 146.52 MHz sitting right in the middle as the national 2m FM calling frequency.

T1B05.explanation: Technicians can transmit digital modes like FT8 on 10 meters (28.000–28.300 MHz) as well as across VHF/UHF bands including 6 meters and 2 meters.

T1B06.explanation: Although Technicians have CW privileges on 80m, 40m, and 15m, the 10-meter band (28.3–28.5 MHz) is the ONLY HF band where Technicians have voice privileges.

T1B07.explanation: The bottom 100 kHz of both 6 meters (50.0–50.1 MHz) and 2 meters (144.0–144.1 MHz) are legally protected weak-signal segments reserved strictly for CW (Morse code).

T1B08.explanation: Where amateurs have secondary status (such as 70 cm, shared with military radar), primary non-amateur stations have priority and you must avoid interfering with them.

T1B09.explanation: Dialing right onto a band edge risks out-of-band transmission from display calibration error, oscillator drift, or modulation sidebands extending past your dial frequency.

T1B10.explanation: Above 50 MHz (from 6 meters upward), SSB voice is permitted in at least part of every amateur band—even right above the narrow CW-only bottom segments.

T1B11.explanation: Across all Technician HF sub-bands below 30 MHz (80m, 40m, 15m CW, and 10m CW/data/SSB), Technicians are capped at 200 watts PEP output.

T1B12.explanation: Above 30 MHz (starting with 6 meters and all VHF/UHF bands), Technicians enjoy the full legal amateur limit of 1,500 watts PEP unless a specific band restriction applies.

T1C01.explanation: The FCC issues new grants for only three classes today—Technician, General, and Amateur Extra; Novice and Advanced are grandfathered classes that can only be renewed.

T1C02.explanation: Any licensed amateur of any class may pick a custom vanity call sign, provided the format belongs to a call sign group eligible for their license class.

T1C03.explanation: International contacts must stick to discussions incidental to amateur radio's purposes and casual personal remarks—conducting business over ham radio is forbidden.

T1C04.explanation: Maintaining a valid email address in the FCC ULS is mandatory; undeliverable FCC correspondence can result in revocation of your station license or suspension of your operator license.

T1C05.explanation: Group D (Technician-eligible) call signs use a 2x3 format—two prefix letters, one region digit, and three suffix letters—like KF1XXX; shorter 1x2 and 2x1 calls require higher classes.

T1C06.explanation: In international waters, a US-documented ship falls under FCC rules, so you may operate maritime mobile aboard it as soon as the vessel's master (captain) approves.

T1C07.explanation: You can file for license renewal starting 90 days (about three months) before your expiration date; applications submitted more than 90 days out are dismissed as premature.

T1C08.explanation: Every new or renewed FCC amateur radio license grant carries a standard 10-year term—lifetime amateur licenses do not exist.

T1C09.explanation: If your license expires, you get a 2-year grace period to renew and rescue your call sign without retaking exams—after two years, the license is gone for good.

T1C10.explanation: After passing your first exam, you must wait until your new call sign actually posts in the FCC's ULS license database before transmitting—your CSCE receipt alone doesn't grant air privileges.

T1C11.explanation: Think of the 2-year grace period like an expired driver's license: you can still renew without retesting, but you may NOT transmit until the renewal actually posts.

T1D01.explanation: US hams may talk to amateurs in any country unless that nation's government formally notifies the ITU (an international UN agency, not the ARRL) that it objects.

T1D02.explanation: Amateur radio is strictly a two-way service, so broadcasting is banned; narrow Part 97 exceptions permit one-way ham bulletins, Morse practice, telemetry, and telecommand.

T1D03.explanation: Ciphers and encryption are prohibited on amateur airwaves, EXCEPT for obscured control commands so unauthorized stations cannot hijack space stations or RC model craft.

T1D04.explanation: Playing music over ham radio is strictly banned, with one space-age exception: background or wake-up music heard during an authorized retransmission of crewed spacecraft audio.

T1D05.explanation: Occasional swap-net announcements to buy, sell, or trade personal amateur radio gear are allowed as long as you aren't doing it on a regular commercial basis.

T1D06.explanation: Indecent or obscene language is flatly prohibited on all amateur bands—even without a printed word list, FCC broadcast decency standards apply on the air.

T1D07.explanation: An auxiliary station acts as an internal point-to-point link—such as relaying audio one-way from a remote hilltop repeater receiver over to the main repeater transmitter.

T1D08.explanation: Hams normally cannot be paid to operate, but Part 97 carves out an exception for paid teachers using an amateur station as part of classroom instruction at a school.

T1D09.explanation: Assisting news gathering or broadcast production is barred unless NO other communication exists AND the message directly protects immediate human life or property.

T1D10.explanation: Part 97 defines broadcasting by its intended audience: any transmission meant for reception by the general public rather than licensed amateurs.

T1D11.explanation: Telecommand of model craft (up to 1 watt with a call-sign label on the transmitter) is the sole situation where an amateur transmitter may operate without on-air station ID.

T1D12.explanation: Even brief tune-ups or antenna test transmissions are subject to normal station ID rules—you must still identify your transmitting station on the air.

T1E01.explanation: An amateur station may NEVER transmit without a control operator—even an unattended repeater under automatic control has a designated human control operator legally in charge.

T1E02.explanation: Working satellites requires no special Extra ticket or AMSAT badge—any ham whose license covers the satellite's uplink frequency (often 2m or 70cm) can be control operator.

T1E03.explanation: The station licensee owns legal responsibility for the station hardware and therefore decides who is designated as the station's control operator.

T1E04.explanation: Transmitting privileges always follow the active control operator's license class—not the station owner's class or whoever else happens to be standing in the room.

T1E05.explanation: A station's control point is wherever the control operator actually performs the control function—whether sitting right at the radio desk or logged in over the internet miles away.

T1E06.explanation: Outside an emergency, you can never serve as control operator beyond your own license privileges; to operate in an Extra segment, an Extra licensee must act as the control operator.

T1E07.explanation: When someone else acts as control operator at your station, the FCC holds BOTH the control operator and the station licensee equally responsible for proper operation.

T1E08.explanation: Automatic control uses built-in devices and procedures to keep transmissions legal without a live operator at the control point—unattended repeater operation is the classic example.

T1E09.explanation: Part 97 permits ANY amateur station to be operated by remote control, provided a reliable control link lets the control operator shut down transmissions when needed.

T1E10.explanation: Operating your home rig over the internet puts the control point away from the transmitter, which is remote control (steering an RC plane by radio is telecommand, not remote control).

T1E11.explanation: Part 97 defines the control operator as the licensed amateur designated by the station licensee to be responsible for all transmissions and FCC rule compliance at that station.

T1F01.explanation: Holding an FCC station license carries an open-door condition: you must make your station and records available at any time upon request by an FCC representative.

T1F02.explanation: Tactical labels like 'Race Headquarters' make event coordination clearer, but they never replace your FCC call sign—you still must ID every 10 minutes and at the end.

T1F03.explanation: Watch out for the 'beginning of contact' trap: Part 97 requires your call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the very end—not legally at the start!

T1F04.explanation: You can converse in any shared language on phone, but your spoken call sign identification must always be given clearly in English.

T1F05.explanation: On voice (phone) transmissions, you may legally identify using either spoken English phone OR CW (Morse code)—which is why voice repeaters can send automatic Morse IDs.

T1F06.explanation: When separating your call sign from a self-assigned portable indicator on voice, Part 97 explicitly accepts 'stroke,' 'slant,' or 'slash' interchangeably.

T1F07.explanation: Letting an unlicensed guest talk over your mic to another country is international third-party traffic, which is legal only if the US has a third-party agreement with that nation.

T1F08.explanation: Third-party communications doesn't mean three hams in a roundtable—it means one control operator passing a message (voice, text, or spoken live) on behalf of another person.

T1F09.explanation: A repeater listens on an input frequency and simultaneously retransmits that exact signal on a different output frequency, dramatically extending handheld and mobile range.

T1F10.explanation: An automatic repeater isn't blamed if a user transmits profanity or out-of-bounds audio into it; accountability rests squarely on the control operator of the originating station.

T1F11.explanation: To qualify for an FCC club station license grant, a club must have at least four members—it does not need ARRL affiliation or an Extra-class trustee.

T2A01.explanation: On the 2-meter band (144–148 MHz), repeaters use a standard plus or minus 600 kHz (0.6 MHz) frequency separation between transmit and receive.

T2A02.explanation: Memorize 146.520 MHz ('one-four-six five-two')—it is the nationwide 2-meter FM simplex calling channel where travelers and hikers monitor for direct radio-to-radio calls.

T2A03.explanation: Because the 70-centimeter UHF band (420–450 MHz) is 30 MHz wide, repeaters there separate input and output by a roomy plus or minus 5 MHz offset.

T2A04.explanation: Calling a specific friend on a repeater is straightforward: state their call sign first to get their attention, then identify with your own call sign—never call 'CQ' or 'break, break.'

T2A05.explanation: When answering a 'CQ,' always lead with the calling station's call sign so they know you are replying to them, followed immediately by your own call sign.

T2A06.explanation: When tuning around simplex or HF SSB without a repeater, repeating 'CQ' a few times followed by 'this is [your call sign]' and pausing to listen invites anyone nearby to answer.

T2A07.explanation: Repeater offset is simply the frequency split (such as 600 kHz on 2m or 5 MHz on 70cm) between the repeater's transmit output frequency and its receive input frequency.

T2A08.explanation: Think of 'CQ' as sounding like 'seek you'—it is the universal radio procedural signal meaning 'calling any station' for a general contact.

T2A09.explanation: On local FM repeaters where operators casually monitor a quiet channel, you skip long 'CQ' calls and simply give your call sign followed by 'listening' or 'monitoring.'

T2A10.explanation: Beyond broad legal FCC rules, a band plan is a voluntary community guideline that neatly separates repeaters, simplex channels, digital modes, and weak-signal work to prevent clashes.

T2A11.explanation: Simplex ('single-frequency' direct mode) means both stations transmit and receive directly on the exact same frequency without going through an offset repeater.

T2B01.explanation: Hitting 'Reverse' flips your RX/TX split so you listen directly on the repeater's input frequency—if you can still hear the other station clearly, you're close enough to move to simplex!

T2B02.explanation: CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System, often called a PL tone) transmits a quiet sub-audible tone below 300 Hz along with your voice to unlock a repeater's receiver.

T2B03.explanation: A linked repeater network connects multiple repeaters via RF or internet links so a signal heard on any single repeater is simultaneously broadcast out of every repeater in the system.

T2B04.explanation: If you hear a repeater's output fine, your receive frequency works—so failing to wake it up almost always comes down to a transmit mismatch: wrong offset, wrong CTCSS tone, or wrong DCS code.

T2B05.explanation: Speaking too loudly over-deviates an FM signal, pushing its instantaneous frequency swing wider than the receiver's IF filter so your voice clips and drops out completely on loud syllables.

T2B06.explanation: DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency)—the familiar telephone keypad touch-tones on your mic or handheld—sends one row tone and one column tone simultaneously to trigger repeater commands.

T2B07.explanation: Joining a digital repeater talkgroup (like 'Statewide' or 'TAC 310') requires no registration paperwork—you just program that talkgroup's numeric ID code into your digital transceiver.

T2B08.explanation: No operator or net ever owns exclusive rights to a ham frequency—if two stations accidentally interfere on the same channel, they should courteously negotiate sharing or shifting frequency.

T2B09.explanation: Band plans carve out dedicated simplex channels so nearby stations can talk directly radio-to-radio instead of tying up a wide-coverage repeater that dozens of others share.

T2B10.explanation: Memory hook: QRM = Man-Made interference from other radio stations, while QRN = Natural static noise like thunderstorms.

T2B11.explanation: Memory hook: QSY = 'Shift Your frequency'—used whenever announcing or suggesting a move to a different frequency or simplex channel.

T2B12.explanation: On DMR digital repeaters, the Color Code (numbered 0–15) serves the exact same gatekeeper role as an analog CTCSS tone—your radio must send the matching Color Code to access the repeater.

T2B13.explanation: Squelch acts as an automatic audio gate that mutes annoying background static when a channel is idle and unmutes the speaker as soon as an incoming signal exceeds the threshold.

T2B14.explanation: In DMR digital radio, a talkgroup ID filters shared repeater timeslots into virtual chat rooms so operators monitoring one group aren't interrupted by unrelated conversations.

T2C01.explanation: Classic exam trap: FCC Part 97 rules ALWAYS apply to every US amateur station—operating for ARES, RACES, or FEMA never overrides FCC regulations.

T2C02.explanation: A Net Control Station (NCS) acts like a meeting moderator—calling the net to order, taking check-ins, and directing who speaks next so stations don't step on each other.

T2C03.explanation: Uncommon names, medications, or street spellings get garbled easily on noisy voice channels, so operators spell unusual words aloud using the standard ITU phonetic alphabet.

T2C04.explanation: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) is a formal FCC Part 97 service established specifically for government civil-defense communications during national emergencies.

T2C05.explanation: In net operations, 'traffic' means formal written messages (radiograms) originated, relayed, or delivered systematically between amateur stations.

T2C06.explanation: ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service) consists of licensed hams who voluntarily register their skills and gear for public-service disaster and community event communications.

T2C07.explanation: Directed nets prevent pileups by following one strict discipline: hold your mic and transmit ONLY when invited by Net Control, unless breaking in with urgent emergency traffic.

T2C08.explanation: Winlink ('Global Radio Email') routes real internet email over HF and VHF/UHF radio links using callsign-based email addresses, keeping critical messages flowing during grid outages.

T2C09.explanation: Only when human life or property faces immediate danger—and normal communications are unavailable—may a control operator step outside their license class's normal frequency privileges.

T2C10.explanation: The preamble at the top of a formal radiogram carries administrative tracking data (message number, precedence, origin station, word check, place, and filing time/date)—not the recipient's address.

T2C11.explanation: The 'check' in a radiogram header is simply the exact count of words (or word equivalents) in the message text so receiving operators can verify no words were lost along the relay.

T2C12.explanation: Memory hook: C in RACES = Civil defense! Unlike voluntary ARES or SKYWARN weather spotting, RACES requires formal enrollment/certification by a government civil defense agency.

T1A.title: Purpose, FCC Rules & Coordination
T1A.subtitle: Why the Amateur Radio Service exists, how your license becomes official, and how repeaters and beacons stay organized.

cards.heading: Part 97 & Getting Officially Licensed
cards.body: The **FCC** regulates the U.S. Amateur Radio Service under **Part 97** to advance technical and communication skills in the radio art—not for mass personal chat like CB or FRS. Once you pass your exam, the FCC sends an **email link** to download your grant, and you are officially licensed as soon as your call sign appears in the **FCC ULS database**.
bullets: **Regulator:** The **FCC** enforces Part 97 (the ARRL is a private club, not a government agency)
**Official proof:** Appearing in the **FCC ULS database** (not your exam-day paper CSCE)
**License delivery:** **Email from the FCC** with a download link

cards.heading: Beacons, Space & Frequency Coordinators
cards.body: Part 97 sets clear boundaries for specialized stations while letting local hams self-organize repeater channels. Local repeater-eligible amateurs select a **Volunteer Frequency Coordinator** to recommend repeater and auxiliary frequencies.
bullets: **10m HF beacons:** Automatically controlled propagation beacons live at **`28.200–28.300 MHz`**
**Space station:** Any amateur station located **more than `50 km`** above Earth's surface
**RACES control operator:** Requires both an FCC ham license AND **civil defense enrollment certification**

cards.heading: On-Air Conduct & Phonetics
cards.body: Good operating keeps shared spectrum clear and intelligible for everyone. The FCC **encourages** phonetic alphabets on voice to clarify call signs and strictly bans intentional jamming.
bullets: **Phonetic alphabet:** **Encouraged** (not required) on phone emissions
**Strictly prohibited:** **Willful or malicious interference** on any frequency

T1B.title: Technician Frequencies, Modes & Power
T1B.subtitle: Where Technicians can use voice and digital modes, contact the ISS, and how much power you may run.

cards.heading: Your HF Gateway: The 10-Meter Band
cards.body: Below `30 MHz` (HF), Technicians are limited to **`200 watts` PEP** and get CW on parts of 80m, 40m, 15m, and 10m. However, **10 meters is the ONLY HF band** where Technicians enjoy voice privileges!
bullets: **Technician HF phone (SSB):** **`28.300 MHz` to `28.500 MHz`** on **10 meters only**
**Digital modes (FT8):** Authorized for Technicians on **10 meters, 6 meters, and 2 meters**
**HF power cap:** **`200 watts` PEP** maximum in Technician HF segments

cards.heading: VHF/UHF Bands, CW Windows & Full Power
cards.body: Above `30 MHz`, Technicians unlock full privileges—including **`1500 watts` PEP** power, contacting astronauts aboard the **ISS** on VHF without NASA paperwork, and SSB voice in at least part of every band above `50 MHz`.
bullets: **Band anchors:** **`52.525 MHz`** is in **6 meters** (`50–54 MHz`); **`146.52 MHz`** is in **2 meters** (`144–148 MHz`)
**CW-only sub-bands:** Bottom `100 kHz` of 6m (**`50.0–50.1 MHz`**) and 2m (**`144.0–144.1 MHz`**)
**VHF/UHF power cap:** **`1500 watts` PEP** above `30 MHz` (except specific band limits)

cards.heading: Band Edges & Secondary Allocations
cards.body: Smart operators stay safely inside band boundaries and respect shared spectrum rules where amateurs are secondary users.
bullets: **Stay off exact band edges:** Guards against **display calibration error**, **frequency drift**, and **modulation sidebands** spilling out-of-band
**Secondary bands:** Non-amateur primary stations operate there—you **must avoid interfering** with them

T1C.title: License Classes, Call Signs & Renewals
T1C.subtitle: Modern license classes, Technician call sign formats, international operating, and renewal timelines.

cards.heading: License Classes & Call Sign Rules
cards.body: The FCC currently issues new licenses for just **three classes**: **Technician, General, and Amateur Extra**. Once your first grant posts in the **FCC license database**, you can transmit immediately and even apply for a custom vanity call sign.
bullets: **Vanity call signs:** Available to **any licensed amateur** (within class-eligible format groups)
**Group D Technician format:** `2×3` call signs like **`KF1XXX`** (2 letters, 1 number, 3 letters)
**First transmission:** Wait until your license grant **appears in the FCC's license database**

cards.heading: Key License Numbers: 10 Years, 90 Days, 2 Years
cards.body: Keeping your license active and your email current in ULS protects your operating privileges. If FCC emails bounce, your station license can be **revoked** or your operator license **suspended**.
bullets: **Normal term:** **10 years**, renewable starting **90 days** before expiration
**Expired grace period:** **2 years** to renew without retesting—**NO transmitting** until renewed!
**Unreachable email penalty:** **Revocation** of station license or **suspension** of operator license

cards.heading: International Contacts & Maritime Waters
cards.body: An FCC amateur license lets you talk across borders and even operate at sea when following simple jurisdiction rules.
bullets: **International topics:** Hobby-incidental talk and **remarks of a personal character** (never business)
**International waters:** Legal aboard a **US-documented vessel** with the **master's permission**

T1D.title: Authorized & Prohibited Transmissions
T1D.subtitle: What Part 97 bans on the air—and the narrow exceptions for spacecraft music, model craft, and classroom teachers.

cards.heading: Core On-Air Prohibitions
cards.body: Amateur radio is a non-commercial, two-way service—not a public radio station. **Broadcasting** (transmissions intended for the **general public**) and **indecent or obscene language** are strictly prohibited.
bullets: **Banned one-way mode:** **Broadcasting** (bulletins, Morse practice, telemetry, and telecommand are allowed)
**Prohibited countries:** Only nations whose administration notified the **ITU** that it objects
**Encoded/encrypted messages:** Permitted **only** for control commands to **space stations or model craft**

cards.heading: Four Narrow Exceptions Tested on the Exam
cards.body: Part 97 bans music, commercial sales, paid operating, and media gathering—except in four very specific situations that exam writers love to ask about.
bullets: **Music on phone:** Only when incidental to authorized **manned spacecraft** retransmissions
**Paid control operator:** Allowed when part of **classroom instruction** at an educational institution
**Equipment sales & news:** Occasional **amateur gear** swaps (not regular); media help **only** for **immediate safety of life or property** with no other means

cards.heading: Auxiliary Links & Identification Exceptions
cards.body: Almost every transmission—including brief on-the-air **test transmissions**—requires station identification, with just one low-power remote-control exception.
bullets: **No on-air ID needed:** Only when transmitting signals to **control model craft**
**Auxiliary station:** Sends one-way links inside a repeater system (e.g., **remote receiver to main transmitter**)

T1E.title: Control Operators & Station Control
T1E.subtitle: Who is legally in charge of a transmitting station, how privileges work, and remote vs. automatic control.

cards.heading: Who Controls the Station & Sets Privileges
cards.body: An amateur station may **never** transmit without a **control operator**—the licensed amateur designated by the **station licensee** to ensure FCC compliance. If a guest operates your station, **both** of you share responsibility.
bullets: **Frequency privileges:** Determined solely by the **control operator's license class**
**Shared accountability:** Both the **control operator AND the station licensee** are responsible
**Extra sub-bands:** Outside emergencies, a Technician may be control operator there **at no time**

cards.heading: Control Points, Remote & Automatic Control
cards.body: The **control point** is the physical or virtual spot where the control operator performs the control function. Modern Part 97 rules allow **any station** to be remotely controlled.
bullets: **Remote control example:** **Operating the station over the internet** (allowed for **any station**)
**Automatic control example:** Unattended **repeater operation**

cards.heading: Satellite Control & Exam Shortcuts
cards.body: Don't fall for distractors claiming you need an Extra Class ticket or special certifications to work amateur satellites.
bullets: **Satellite control operator:** **Any amateur** allowed to transmit on the **satellite uplink frequency** (usually 2m or 70cm)
**No control operator allowed?** **Never**—even automatic repeaters have a designated control operator

T1F.title: Station ID, Third-Party Traffic & Clubs
T1F.subtitle: The 10-minute English ID rule, portable indicators, international guests on the mic, repeaters, and club grants.

cards.heading: Mastering the 10-Minute Station ID Rule
cards.body: Whether chatting casually or using tactical call signs like "Race Headquarters," you must transmit your FCC-assigned call sign **at least every 10 minutes during and at the end** of a communication.
bullets: **Exam trap:** Identifying at the *beginning* of a contact is **not** required by Part 97!
**Phone ID rules:** Must be in **English**, sent via **CW or phone** emission
**Portable indicators:** **"Stroke," "slant," and "slash"** (e.g., `KL7CC slash W3`) are all acceptable

cards.heading: Third-Party Traffic & Repeaters
cards.body: **Third-party communications** are messages passed between control operators on behalf of another person. Meanwhile, a **repeater station** simultaneously retransmits another station's signal on a different channel.
bullets: **Foreign third-party traffic:** Allowed **only** with countries holding a **U.S. third-party agreement**
**Repeater rule violations:** The **control operator of the originating station** is accountable (not the repeater owner)

cards.heading: FCC Inspections & Club Licenses
cards.body: Station records and hardware remain subject to FCC oversight, and local radio clubs can apply for their own shared club call sign.
bullets: **FCC inspection:** Station and records must be available **at any time upon request** by an FCC representative
**Club station license:** Requires a club with **at least four members**

T2A.title: Repeater Offsets, Simplex & Calling
T2A.subtitle: Standard 2m and 70cm offsets, the 146.520 MHz calling frequency, and clean on-air calling procedures.

cards.heading: Simplex vs. Repeater Offsets
cards.body: **Simplex** means transmitting and receiving on the **exact same frequency** directly between radios. Repeaters use a **repeater offset**—the difference between the repeater's transmit and receive frequencies.
bullets: **2m national FM simplex calling frequency:** **`146.520 MHz`**
**2-meter repeater offset:** **`±600 kHz`** (`0.6 MHz`)
**70-centimeter repeater offset:** **`±5 MHz`**

cards.heading: How to Make & Answer Calls Cleanly
cards.body: Whenever calling a specific station or answering **`CQ`** ("**Calling any station**"), always transmit **the other station's call sign first, followed by your call sign**. Match your calling style to repeater vs. simplex operation.
bullets: **Looking for a repeater chat:** Say **your call sign followed by "listening"** (don't call `CQ` on FM repeaters)
**Seeking any phone contact off-repeater:** Repeat **`CQ`** a few times + "this is" + **your call sign**, then pause to listen
**Calling a known station:** Say **their call sign, then identify with your call sign** (skip "break, break")

cards.heading: Voluntary Band Plans
cards.body: FCC rules only divide bands into broad license and mode segments; the amateur community organizes the rest cooperatively.
bullets: **Band plan definition:** A **voluntary guideline** for organizing modes and activities (repeaters, simplex, satellites) within a band

T2B.title: Tones, Digital Talkgroups & Operating Tips
T2B.subtitle: CTCSS, DTMF, DMR Color Codes and talkgroups, repeater troubleshooting, and essential Q-signals.

cards.heading: Analog Repeater Controls & Tones
cards.body: **Squelch** mutes background static when no signal is present, while **CTCSS** adds a **sub-audible tone** under your voice to open a repeater's squelch. **Linked repeater networks** retransmit one repeater's input across every repeater in the system.
bullets: **`Reverse` button:** Listens on a repeater's **input frequency** to see if you can reach the other station on simplex
**`DTMF` tones:** **Two simultaneous audio tones** (keypad touch-tones) used to send commands to a repeater
**Simplex channels:** Designated in band plans so nearby stations **don't tie up a repeater**

cards.heading: DMR Digital Repeaters & Troubleshooting
cards.body: DMR repeaters require a programmed **Color Code** (access code) and route conversations using **talkgroups** so listeners only hear traffic meant for their chosen group.
bullets: **Joining a talkgroup:** Simply **program your radio with the group's ID or code**
**Can hear a repeater, can't key it up?** Check **improper offset**, **wrong CTCSS tone**, or **wrong DCS code**
**FM audio dropping out on voice peaks?** **You are talking too loudly** (over-deviating past the receiver filter)

cards.heading: Frequency Sharing & Must-Know Q-Signals
cards.body: No ham has preemptive ownership of a frequency—when two stations interfere on the same channel, they should **negotiate continued use** politely.
bullets: **`QRM`:** Receiving **M**an-made interference from other stations (`QRN` = natural static)
**`QSY`:** Changing frequency (**S**hift **Y**our frequency)

T2C.title: Emergencies, Nets & Formal Traffic
T2C.subtitle: When emergency rules apply, ARES vs. RACES, directed net etiquette, Winlink email, and radiogram headers.

cards.heading: Emergency Rules & Agency Organizations
cards.body: **FCC Part 97 rules ALWAYS apply**—even during disasters or exercises! However, control operators may transmit outside their license class's frequency privileges **only** when **immediate safety of human life or protection of property** is at stake.
bullets: **ARES:** Licensed volunteers who **register their qualifications and equipment** for public-service duty
**RACES:** Official Part 97 **civil defense** emergency service requiring **certification by a civil defense agency**

cards.heading: Directed Net Etiquette
cards.body: During a net, the **Net Control Station (NCS)** calls the net to order and directs all communications between check-ins so stations never talk over one another.
bullets: **Golden net rule:** Unless reporting an emergency, **transmit ONLY when directed** by Net Control
**Unusual words:** Spell tricky names or terms aloud using a **standard phonetic alphabet**

cards.heading: Formal Traffic, Radiograms & Winlink
cards.body: In net jargon, **traffic** refers to **formal messages** relayed systematically between stations, either by voice radiogram or digital email.
bullets: **Radiogram `preamble`:** Contains metadata needed to **track the message**
**Radiogram `check`:** Exact **number of words** (or word equivalents) in the message text
**`Winlink`:** Relays digital messages using **email addresses based on amateur callsigns**
